# Hardware-Bringup skill

First-power to working-firmware: staged board validation, clock/power/clock-tree
verification, memory testing, peripheral checkout, and the bring-up report that
promotes a board from unknown to trusted.

## 1. Purpose and scope

**Purpose.** Prove the hardware matches its model (`hardware-architecture` HSI)
incrementally — never powering a full system blind — and deliver a board software
can trust with documented deviations.

**In scope.** Bring-up planning and staging, power-rail sequencing checks, clock
verification, JTAG/SWD connectivity, memory tests, peripheral loopbacks,
bootloader porting to new hardware, and the bring-up report.

**Non-goals.** Schematic design (see `hardware-architecture`) and production
test fixtures. Ends at a board running application firmware with a signed
bring-up report.

## 2. Normative sources (high confidence)

| # | Reference | Version / status | Scope | Source |
|---|-----------|------------------|-------|--------|
| 1 | JTAG IEEE 1149.1 | 2013 (3rd ed.) | Boundary scan, connectivity verification | `https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/1149-1/4244/` |
| 2 | ARM CoreSight | Current architecture spec | Debug/trace infrastructure for bring-up observability | `https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ihi0029/latest/` |
| 3 | JEDEC JESD47 | Current (stress-test-driven qualification) | Component stress methodology informing board-level stress | `https://www.jedec.org/standards-documents/docs/jesd-47` |

## 3. Staging rules — earn each next step

1. **Power first, alone.** Rails sequenced per design with current-limited
   supply; verify levels, sequencing, and ripple at the load before any clock
   or silicon runs. Shorts found here cost minutes; found later cost boards.
2. **Clocks second.** Oscillators and PLLs measured (frequency, stability,
   jitter class) before any synchronous peripheral is trusted.
3. **Debug third.** JTAG/SWD chain integrity, boundary-scan connectivity, and
   memory-mapped access to key registers — the observation path for
   everything after.
4. **Memories fourth.** SRAM/stack patterns, flash erase/program/verify, DRAM
   calibration and marching/bitfade tests at voltage and temperature corners.
5. **Peripherals fifth.** UART loopback → timers → GPIO → buses (I2C/SPI at
   low speed first, then rated speed with scope captures) → complex IP
   (Ethernet, USB, display).
6. **Bootloader last.** Port the bootloader (`bootloader` skill) only onto a
   board that passed stages 1–5; bootloader failures on unproven hardware
   waste debug effort on two unknowns at once.

## 4. Rules

- One variable at a time: each stage passes in isolation before combining.
- Golden captures: scope/logic-analyzer traces of working rails, clocks, and
  buses archived as reference for regression when later stages misbehave.
- Deviation log: every hardware surprise (wrong strap, weak rail, errata hit)
  recorded with software impact and disposition — this log becomes the
  bring-up report appendix.

## 5. Release gates (blocking)

1. All six stages pass with recorded measurements.
2. Bring-up report signed: measurements, golden captures, deviation log with
   dispositions, HSI corrections fed back to `hardware-architecture`.
3. Board revision uniquely identifiable by firmware at runtime (ID resistors,
   EEPROM, or OTP — never "we know which batch this is").

## 6. Verification of this skill (Phase 4 gate)

- References carry number + version + scope + URL (§2).
